title: Does the Voice Change the Grade? A Causal Audit of Speaker-Identity Bias in Audio-LLM Judges
paper_type: analysis / empirical audit (controlled behavioral study of deployed models)
summary: The authors author 24 interview-style question-answer pairs, freeze the answer text, and render each answer with a text-to-speech model in four accents (American, British, Indian, Nigerian English) crossed with two speaker genders, yielding 192 clips whose lexical content is identical within an item. Two audio-input judges, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3.6 Flash, score every clip on a 0-100 rubric at temperature zero, one clip per call, blind to the purpose of the study. Across six accent-by-judge comparisons, one survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction: Gemini 3.1 Pro scores Indian-accented renderings 2.5 points lower than the identical American-accented answer (95% CI -4.06 to -0.94, p = 0.005, d_z = -0.44), while Gemini 3.6 Flash shows no such shift (-0.04, p = 1.0). A decomposition arm regrades the same items from the judge's own transcript and from the frozen gold transcript and finds no significant penalty in either transcript mode, which the authors read as localizing the bias in the acoustic channel. A second axis testing five delivery perturbations (filled pauses, faster and slower speech, 8kHz codec, pink noise) returns null under both judges and both prompt arms, and the authors explicitly report this as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no effect.
central_claim: When an audio-input LLM grades a spoken answer, the score can depend causally on the speaker's accent even with the words held identical (Gemini 3.1 Pro: -2.5 points for Indian-accented English), the effect is judge-specific rather than a vendor-wide property, and it is removable by grading from a transcript, which localizes it in the acoustic channel.
strengths: The core manipulation is genuinely causal and cleanly specified: text is frozen per item and only the rendering varies, so within-item score differences cannot be attributed to answer content. This is the right design for the question and is executed as described.

Statistical reporting is well above ICLR norms: bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples) on every cell, two-sided sign-flip permutation tests (20,000 permutations), paired effect sizes, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all six accent-judge tests with the rank-1 critical value stated explicitly (0.0083). Only ~40% of ICLR papers show error bars and ~6% run significance tests.

Unusual and creditable honesty about nulls and failures. Section 4.3 and Figure 6 report the entire delivery axis as null and the authors refuse to read it as evidence of no effect, citing the planning-stage power analysis. Section 3.1 reports a failed first calibration (mean 94.3/100, SD 4.5, ceiling effect) that forced a redesign, and Section 3.3 reports that 28 of 33 initial WER-gate failures were artifacts of the transcribing model, not the audio.

The pre-registered direction was violated and the authors say so: Nigerian-accented answers trend positive under both judges, the opposite of the predicted global-South penalty, and this is reported rather than buried.

The related-work positioning (Section 2) is unusually precise, distinguishing this design from AudioJudge, BiasInEar, ParaPairAudioBench, Satish et al., and Labroo et al. on the specific axis of who is being judged and what the outcome is, rather than by generic topical proximity.
Figures 1, 3, and 4 are genuinely explanatory rather than decorative; Figure 4 in particular makes the three-way grading-mode comparison legible at a glance.

weaknesses.text: FATAL CONFOUND: accent is confounded with synthesis quality, and the rubric explicitly scores clarity. The accent conditions are produced by prompting a TTS model with a natural-language style instruction. The only manipulation check verifies that a classifier can identify the intended accent in 8 of 8 clips; nothing verifies that the four accent renderings are matched on naturalness, intelligibility, pronunciation accuracy, or artifact rate. The judge's rubric asks for 'correctness, completeness, helpfulness, and clarity.' If the synthetic Indian-English rendering is less intelligible or more artifact-laden than the synthetic American rendering, a 2.5-point clarity deduction is correct rubric-following, not demographic bias. The paper's headline framing ('the score can move with the voice', 'partly scoring the speaker rather than the answer') requires ruling this out and does not.

FATAL GENERALITY: one voice per accent-by-gender cell means there is no voice-level replication. Eight distinct synthetic voices carry the entire accent claim. The bootstrap CI resamples over the 24 items, so it quantifies uncertainty about generalizing to new answers, not to new speakers. The estimand as analyzed is 'the effect of these two particular synthetic Indian-accented voices,' which is not the estimand the title, abstract, and conclusion claim. A voice-level random effect (or simply multiple voices per cell) is required before 'Indian accent lowers the score' is licensed. Similarly, the reported gender main effect is a comparison of two specific voices and cannot speak to gender.

The decomposition claim is inferred from a difference in significance rather than from a test of a difference. Section 4.2 and the conclusion assert the penalty 'lives in the acoustic channel' because audio is significant (p = 0.006) while the two transcript modes are not (p = 0.14, p = 0.51). No accent-by-grading-mode interaction test is reported. With the transcript arms at roughly half the item count, this is exactly the pattern low power produces regardless of whether the underlying effect differs. Note also that the own-transcript CI is [0.00, 3.96], i.e. borderline significant in the opposite direction, which the paper reads as 'the penalty is gone' rather than as a signal that something unmodelled is happening in the transcript route.

Internal numerical inconsistency between Table 1 and Table 2. Table 1 reports the Gemini 3.1 Pro Indian shift as -2.50, CI [-4.06, -0.94], p = 0.005 at n = 48 paired comparisons. Table 2's 'Audio' row reports -2.50, CI [-4.06, -0.94], p = 0.006 with a caption stating n = 24 on a stratified subset of 12 of the 24 items. Two different subsets producing an identical point estimate and an identical bootstrap CI to two decimals is not plausible; either the decomposition audio arm silently reuses the full Axis A data and the caption's n is wrong, or numbers were transcribed between tables. Either way the decomposition arm's stated design does not match its stated numbers, which undermines the paper's second headline finding.

Single-vendor evidence base for a claim about audio-LLM judges in general. Both judges are Gemini, the TTS is Gemini, and the accent manipulation check classifier is Gemini. The authors flag the judge and manipulation-check circularity in Section 5, but the framing throughout ('every deployed pipeline listed in the introduction is partly scoring the speaker') generalizes far past two sibling models from one company evaluating one company's synthetic speech. The judge-disagreement contribution is weakened by the same issue: two models from one vendor disagreeing is closer to a version-difference observation than to a finding about judge families.

Effect size is small and its practical consequence is never evaluated. The 2.5-point shift sits on a score distribution with SD 17.0, i.e. roughly 0.15 population SD. The paper does not report how many item-level decisions this flips, how it propagates to a pass/fail threshold, to a candidate ranking, or to a leaderboard ordering, despite the introduction motivating the work entirely through such deployed pipelines. Without that, 'what changes if all of this is true' is unanswered.

Pre-registration is claimed in the abstract and Section 4.1 but no registry link, timestamp, hash, or appendix documents it, and the paper is double-blind with no anonymized artifact. As stated it is an unverifiable assertion. Likewise there is no code, data, prompt, or rubric release statement anywhere, no reproducibility statement, and no ethics statement, all of which are expected at ICLR for a study of demographic bias.

No appendix and no supporting material of any kind. The exact judge rubric text, the two prompt arms, the 24 items, the TTS style instructions, the 8-clip manipulation-check protocol, the WER-gate prompts, and the power analysis referenced in Section 4.3 are all described in prose but never shown. A reader cannot assess whether the rubric's 'clarity' criterion, the accent style instruction, or the exclusion of 5 of 120 conditions drives the result.

One clip per call at temperature zero with no repeat measurements means judge self-consistency is never measured. API-level nondeterminism at temperature zero is well documented; without a test-retest estimate, an unknown share of the within-item variance is measurement noise of unknown magnitude, and the paired CIs assume it away.

Drafting errors that a reviewer will read as haste. The abstract announces 'Two findings are co-equal. First... Second...' and then jumps to 'Fourth, we test five delivery perturbations' with no third. The conclusion ends with 'already scoped in this project's experiment plan,' Section 5 cites a '$20 compute budget,' and Section 3.4 says a third judge remains a 'planned addition' — the paper reads in several places as an internal progress report rather than a submission.

The noise perturbation uses synthesized pink noise as a stand-in for multi-talker babble, which the authors concede is not equivalent. Since the delivery axis is entirely null anyway, this mostly compounds the axis's uninformativeness rather than causing a wrong conclusion.

missing_experiment: A naturalness- and intelligibility-matched control that separates accent identity from synthesis quality. Concretely: obtain independent per-clip intelligibility/MOS ratings (human listeners, or at minimum a non-Gemini model plus a non-Gemini ASR word-error rate per accent condition) and re-estimate the Indian-accent shift with that quality score as a covariate. If the -2.5 penalty survives conditioning on intelligibility, the bias claim is established; if it does not, the paper has measured a TTS artifact. The authors' own named next step — replicating on real L2-ARCTIC recordings with multiple speakers per accent — would accomplish the same thing and would simultaneously fix the one-voice-per-cell problem, and its absence is what a reviewer will notice first.

format_audit.verdict_vs_norms: Seven pages of body plus three of references, versus an ICLR median of 25 pages; 6 figures and 2 tables versus norms of 11.5 and 8.7. There is no appendix at all, which is atypical to the point of being conspicuous — prompts, rubric text, item bank, power analysis, and pre-registration all go undocumented. The paper is above norm on error bars (present everywhere, versus 40.2% of accepted papers) and well above norm on significance testing with multiplicity correction (6.1% of accepted papers). Table 2 functions as a grading-mode ablation, satisfying that norm in substance. Figure polish is high and the page-2 teaser is genuinely informative. Net: statistically better dressed than the median accepted paper, but roughly a third of its substance, and the missing appendix converts several methodological claims into assertions.

venue_fit.reasoning: Topically this sits near ICLR's LLM safety/robustness and audio-language-model clusters, which together are a real but modest slice of the program (~2.5% for safety/robustness in the latest year), and evaluation-of-judges work does appear at ICLR. But the paper contributes no method, no released benchmark or dataset, no theory, and no mechanistic account of why the judge behaves this way — it is a small-n behavioral audit of two closed commercial checkpoints, which is a style ICLR publishes far less often than Interspeech, ACL, or FAccT would. The 24-item, two-model, $20-budget scale reads as a workshop or short-paper contribution at this venue; the same design at ten times the scale with a real-speech arm would fit an ICLR datasets-and-benchmarks or safety track comfortably.

calibration_note: An average of 3.7 falls in the 3.5-4.0 band, where 2.3% of 2,010 real ICLR submissions were accepted; no venue adjustment applies since ICLR is the target, and the usual borderline caveat is weak here — a paper with an unaddressed confound on its headline claim and no voice-level replication is below the noise floor of the accept/reject boundary rather than on it.
what_would_move_to_accept: Break the accent/synthesis-quality confound. Add 3-5 distinct voices per accent-by-gender cell and include an independent intelligibility or MOS covariate (non-Gemini ASR WER per clip is a cheap first pass; human ratings are better). Re-fit with voice as a random effect so the CI generalizes over speakers, not just items. This is the single change that decides whether the paper has a finding at all. Effort: 2-4 weeks, low compute cost, moderate annotation cost.

Replicate on real speech. Complete the L2-ARCTIC registration already described as pending and run the identical protocol on recorded non-native speakers reading matched prompts. This simultaneously anchors ecological validity and supplies multi-speaker replication. Effort: 3-4 weeks, gated on the distributor agreement.

Add a third and fourth judge family from other vendors (an OpenAI audio judge and an open-weight model such as Qwen-Audio or an Ultravox-class model). Without this, the judge-disagreement contribution cannot support the 'which model you pick is not a neutral engineering choice' claim. Effort: 1-2 weeks, small compute.

Test the decomposition claim properly: fit an accent x grading-mode interaction rather than comparing significance across arms, run all three modes on the full 24-item bank at equal n, and resolve the Table 1 / Table 2 numerical inconsistency. Effort: days, no new data if the full bank is regraded.

Scale the item bank to roughly 150 items as in the predecessor design and re-run the delivery axis, so that Axis B either yields a finding or a genuinely powered null with a stated minimum detectable effect. Effort: 2-3 weeks, modest compute.

Quantify downstream consequence: report decision flips at plausible thresholds, rank-order changes on a simulated leaderboard, and pass-rate deltas at a realistic cut score. Effort: days, uses existing data.

Release the artifact and the pre-registration. Anonymized repo with items, prompts, rubric, raw judgment logs, and the analysis script; a registry link with timestamp. Add reproducibility and ethics statements and a full appendix. Effort: days, and it is the cheapest credibility gain available.
Expand to ICLR length with the above, and repair the abstract enumeration and the residual project-report phrasing in Sections 3.4, 5, and 6. Effort: days.
